shows.title: Eric Aho: The Meadow's Edge
shows.description:
Eric Aho returns to the subject of his 2024 show Wild Meadow for a deeper look at the same stretch of Vermont land at sunrise, twilight, and across the turning seasons. The new paintings catch transitional moments — snow just beginning to thaw, fireflies dissolving into summer mist, the last light before full dark — and use them to explore the blurry border between direct observation and invention. In one recurring device, light falls across the meadow in hard geometric shapes that cut against the organic tangle of grasses and wildflowers beneath, so that the paintings hold two ways of seeing in tension at once.

Alongside the meadow paintings are nocturnal forest views and a continuation of Aho's Dutch Meadow series, which reimagines the seventeenth-century Dutch floral still life as a living, glowing tableau set against black ground — flowers, fireflies, and stars all treated as sources of the same light. His yearly Firefly paintings, timed to the insects' brief lifespan, function almost as a diary of successive summers.

The show coincides with the release of Aho's first monograph, published by Rizzoli Electa with an essay by John Yau, marking a useful moment to take stock of a painter who has spent decades finding endless variation within a self-imposed set of subjects: meadow, forest edge, ice, and now, again, meadow.

shows.title: Land, Line, Blood, Memory
shows.description:
Sarah Sense's third solo show with Bruce Silverstein brings together more than twenty new photo-weavings that braid together the artist's own landscape photographs with archival land records, historical images, and maps — a technique she has spent two decades refining, drawing on traditional Chitimacha and Choctaw basketry methods taught to her by her grandmother and by master weaver John Paul Darden. Rivercane, harvested and prepared using ancestral methods, cotton thread, ribbon, and printed bamboo and rice papers all get physically woven into the photographic surface, so the work insists on craft and labor as much as image.

The show is structured around its title's four terms: land as a living source of relationship rather than property, line as the colonial mapping and legal record-keeping that converted stewardship into ownership, blood as the archival documents of Chitimacha and Choctaw land dispossession, and memory as the gaps in the historical record that Sense fills back in with her own photographs of Tahoe, Sequoia, Redwood, and Yosemite. The exhibition also debuts her first Tree Weaving Quilt, a new, more intimate format made collaboratively with her children.

It's dense, materially rich work that turns weaving into a form of historical reclamation — asking who gets to narrate land and memory, and using the literal interlacing of photograph and object to answer that question by hand.

shows.title: The Tesseract
shows.description:
Zio Ziegler's fourth solo show with Almine Rech gathers four distinct bodies of work under one roof: dense, maximalist "illuminated manuscript" paintings; pared-back skeletal monochrome canvases; the biomorphic, totem-like paintings he calls "Essential Figures"; and bronze sculptures that translate those same figures into three dimensions. The Bay Area-raised, mural-trained painter has always worked at a large scale and with an omnivorous visual vocabulary, and here he leans into that range rather than smoothing it out, letting four almost contradictory modes argue with and complete each other across the gallery.

The paintings draw on an unusually literary set of sources for a artist better known for public murals — Ovid's Metamorphoses, the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Bible — filtered through quotations from Masaccio, Rubens, Memling, Picasso, and Rauschenberg's Erased de Kooning Drawing. Recurring imagery of expulsion and transformation (Adam and Eve banished from Eden, figures caught mid-metamorphosis) gives the show a loose narrative undertow, while the monochrome works, inspired partly by black- and red-figure Greek pottery, strip that same mythic content down to bare gesture.

Underneath the historical references, Ziegler is using the show to ask a very current question: what remains distinctly human, and what kind of image-making still matters, in an age of AI-generated visual homogeneity. It's an ambitious, occasionally overstuffed premise for a gallery show, but the four-part structure gives viewers a way in — whether through the maximalist canvases' sheer density of incident, the quieter charge of the monochromes, or the sculptures' blunt physical presence.

shows.title: Germinal
shows.description:
Organized with the Easton Foundation, Germinal zeroes in on a single hinge moment in Louise Bourgeois's long career: the late 1960s, when she left behind the rigid, totemic verticality of her early wood Personages for softer, more visceral forms in plaster, latex, and bronze. The two-floor installation splits by medium — sculpture on the ground floor, drawing on the fourth — and by doing so makes an argument about how Bourgeois actually worked, moving the same handful of forms back and forth between two and three dimensions rather than treating drawing as mere preparation for sculpture.

Downstairs, three large segmented totemic sculptures anchor works from her Germinal (1966–67) and Fingers (1968–71) series, built through repeated pouring, casting, and hand-shaping — clustered protrusions, glove-poured plaster fingers, embedded pins — that read as both growth and accumulation. Upstairs, the atmospheric Cumul drawings from the same years render the same impulse toward repetition as pure contour: cloud-like, cell-like forms that Bourgeois described as a source of calm, "the peaceful side of things," even as the underlying psychic material stayed turbulent.

It's a tightly focused, scholarly show rather than a survey — no Cells, no giant spiders — and it's stronger for the restraint. Seeing the sculptural and graphic vocabularies side by side clarifies something about Bourgeois's method that a broader retrospective tends to blur: that for her, an image wasn't a finished statement but a form to be run through variations in whatever material was at hand.

shows.title: Agita
shows.dates_note: gladstonegallery.com's own exhibitions section loads only via client-side JavaScript and returned no readable listing/dates through this session's fetch tools (render_fetch also unavailable). Dates, address, and hours here are cross-confirmed via the trade platform Ocula's gallery-submitted exhibition record (published Aug 25, 2026) and match Gladstone's other NY location hours; Yaeger's representation by Gladstone is independently confirmed on gladstonegallery.com/artist/joseph-yaeger/.
shows.description:
Joseph Yaeger paints from a working method built on instability: heavily gessoed canvas or linen, scored and misted with water so the surface itself develops unpredictable texture, then layered with translucent watercolor that pools and settles into the disturbed ground. The result is a body of tightly cropped, cinematic images — faces, hands, fragments of objects — that read like stills pulled from a film that doesn't quite exist, rendered with an uncanny, almost hallucinatory clarity.

Agita marks Yaeger's New York solo debut with Gladstone, following a run of attention-getting solo shows in London and Shanghai and a rapidly rising secondary market. His pictures work by fragmentation and cropping, isolating a gesture or expression from any legible narrative context so that the emotional charge of the image feels both intensely specific and strangely unmoored — psychological portraiture stripped of the reassurance of a full scene.

For a painter who has built his reputation on the tension between control and material accident, a full-room presentation at this scale is a real test of how those tightly-wound individual images hold together as a body of work.

shows.title: Jordan Wolfson
shows.description:
Jordan Wolfson's first exhibition with Gagosian in New York brings together a group of new, uniformly scaled sculptures built around found photographs — color and black-and-white images pulled from online sources, personal archives, and academic collections. Wolfson has built a career on works that unsettle viewers by combining familiar image-and-object languages with something slightly off — the animatronic figures, the VR pieces that put you inside acts of violence — and this show's premise, using photographic fragments as raw material for sculpture, continues his interest in how images accrue meaning once they're wrenched out of their original context.

Without a finished checklist yet public, the exact content of the archive Wolfson is drawing on remains something of a mystery, but the pairing of "emblematic" photography with sculptural form suggests another round of his ongoing interrogation of how we process images of history, celebrity, and everyday life. A conversation between Wolfson and novelist Ottessa Moshfegh, appearing in Gagosian's fall Quarterly, should offer more context once the show opens.

Given how rarely Wolfson shows in New York and how consistently his work provokes strong reactions, this is one of the more anticipated openings of the fall season, even with details still emerging.

shows.title: MOTHERS
shows.description:
Inma Barrero's debut exhibition with Lévy Gorvy Dayan is a small, focused presentation of eight ceramic sculptures that treats motherhood and the discipline of ceramics as parallel, intertwined journeys — both processes of shaping something soft and unformed into a lasting structure, both requiring patience with material that resists full control.

Barrero draws on a wide range of historical and geographic reference points in her forms, and the sculptures on view read less like straightforward figuration than like abstracted vessels carrying the weight of that research. It's a quiet, intimate show by gallery standards — eight objects rather than a sprawling installation — and its scale suits the subject: motherhood examined through the slow, hands-on labor of clay rather than through grand gesture.

As a first outing with a gallery known for staging historical surveys of blue-chip estates, MOTHERS is a notable bet on a living artist working in a medium, ceramics, that galleries at this level don't always take seriously as sculpture.

shows.title: Re-membering
shows.description:
Wangari Mathenge's first solo show with Lévy Gorvy Dayan pushes her practice in two new directions at once: it's her first public presentation of sculpture, and it debuts five new paintings, all organized around how culture, memory, and landscape get constructed and dismantled over time. Mathenge has built her reputation on interior scenes of the Kenyan diaspora — domestic spaces filled with pattern, books, and the visual texture of a specific cultural world — and the move into sculpture suggests she's looking for a more physical, dimensional way to hold the same questions about inheritance and belonging.

The title's hyphenation is a clue to the show's method: "re-membering" as both recollection and reassembly, putting fragmented pieces of personal and collective history back together into a legible whole. Given that this is new territory for the artist on two fronts, the show reads as a deliberate expansion rather than a victory lap — a chance to see whether the psychological density of her paintings can carry over into three dimensions.

shows.title: Pierre Soulages: Paintings on Paper
shows.description:
More than twenty works on paper by Pierre Soulages make up this show, most of them never exhibited before — a genuinely rare event for an artist as thoroughly documented as the French painter who spent seven decades investigating black as a generator of light rather than its absence. Organized in collaboration with the artist's widow, Colette Soulages, the exhibition argues for paper as a full-fledged part of his practice rather than a footnote to the large-scale "outrenoir" canvases he's best known for.

Working on paper forced a different relationship to the material than his heavily worked, tool-scraped canvases did, and the works here should make visible a more immediate, exploratory side of an artist whose public reputation rests almost entirely on his monumental black paintings. For anyone who knows Soulages only through museum-scale canvases, this is a chance to see the same lifelong preoccupation with black, texture, and reflected light worked out at an intimate scale.

shows.title: The Khajistan Institute for Advanced Research and Necessary Development
shows.description:
Khajistan, the archive and publishing project devoted to banned, censored, and disappearing media from what its founders call the "Middle World," takes over Recess's storefront for its Session residency, turning the space into a working research institute rather than a finished exhibition. Modeled loosely on a home computer-education center, the installation is built around the construction in public of the Khajistan Portal, a new interface for navigating an archive that will soon run past two million pages of digitized books, magazines, comics, films, and born-digital ephemera collected from North Africa to South Asia.

Because Recess's Session format is explicitly process-based, what's on view will keep shifting over its five-week run: a Reading Room of periodicals and print matter, a Screening Room pulling from documentary, narrative, and popular cinema, and a Born-Digital Archive of memes and social-media material are all being assembled and refined with visitors' input rather than presented as a static display. Material from the digital collection spills into the physical room too, as prints and ephemera pulled from the portal accumulate on the walls over the course of the residency, forming a kind of visitor-authored record of what people searched for and lingered on.

The project is led by Saad Khan, who directs Khajistan's collecting and editorial work, and Joey Chriqui, who designed the Recess installation and leads the archive's exhibition and publishing side, with technologist Amad Ansari building the Portal's back end. It's a rare chance to watch an archive's public interface get built in real time, with open drop-in hours, office-hour sessions, and public working meetings scheduled throughout the run rather than a single opening night.

Given its improvisational, evolving nature, this is a show best visited more than once — early to see the bare bones of the Portal and Reading Room, and again later once the walls have filled in with the material the public itself has helped surface.

shows.title: Proserpina / Devil Chaser
shows.description:
This two-person exhibition pairs Rosemary Mayer and Ree Morton, two artists who were close friends in the 1970s and who each pushed post-minimal sculpture toward something stranger, softer, and more theatrical. Both women found in flowers and plant forms a language for talking about decay, artifice, and feeling, and the show is built around a rare meeting of two major sculptures from 1975 — Mayer's "Proserpina" and Morton's "Devil Chaser" — that were each inspired by botanical imagery and myth.

Around those anchor works, the gallery gathers smaller pieces that flesh out each artist's vocabulary: Mayer's watercolor and colored-pencil studies of fabric and flowers, a recording of her reading from her 1976 book "Passages," and Morton's text-based "Signs of Love" paintings and her Beaux sculptures, which mix cartoonish drawing with wood and glitter. A few objects speak directly to the friendship itself — a flag from Morton's "Something in the Wind" installation dedicated to Mayer, and a Mayer balloon drawing made the year after Morton's early death in 1977 — alongside letters, sketchbooks, and photographs that document their overlapping circles.

It's a quietly moving show for anyone interested in how the feminist and post-minimal generations dealt with sentiment, humor, and craft without apologizing for any of it. Seeing Mayer and Morton's work side by side, rather than folded into larger surveys, makes clear how much they were talking to each other in real time — and how much art history still has to catch up to their strange, tender objects.

shows.title: Faces & Figures
shows.artist: Georg Baselitz, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Willem de Kooning, Eric Fischl, Alberto Giacometti, Martin Kippenberger, Fernand Léger, Joan Miró, Pablo Picasso, Richard Prince, Cindy Sherman, Lynette Yiadom-Boakye
shows.dates_note: Skarstedt's own exhibitions page lists this show only as "Summer 2026," with no specific opening or closing date given.
shows.description:
Skarstedt's Upper East Side townhouse gathers a dozen artists across a century of figuration, hanging a Giacometti oil beside a Cindy Sherman self-portrait, a Basquiat wood panel near a late Léger, and a de Kooning bronze torso in the middle of it all. The premise is loose but pointed: the human face and body as the one subject painters and photographers of wildly different eras and temperaments keep returning to, whether to flatter it, distort it, or interrogate how it's represented.

What makes the checklist interesting is the friction between generations. Kippenberger's sardonic 1992 canvas and Richard Prince's 2012 inkjet-and-oil hybrid sit in the same rooms as Picasso's 1967 Ripolin painting and a 1956 Miró gouache, so the show reads less as a survey than as a series of arguments about what counts as a portrait now. Lynette Yiadom-Boakye's invented sitter is the newest voice in the mix, a reminder that the genre is still being written.

It's a good excuse to see museum-caliber works by blue-chip names in an intimate, salon-style setting rather than a white cube — the kind of show where you can stand close enough to compare brushwork across eighty years in a single glance.

shows.title: A well of night
shows.description:
Thea Djordjadze's first exhibition at Sprüth Magers' New York location treats the gallery's neo-Renaissance rooms as raw material rather than neutral backdrop. The Georgian-born, Berlin-based sculptor has covered the space's dark hardwood floors in pale vinyl, a simple gesture that resets the room's sense of scale and light before a single sculpture is even encountered — typical of an artist who has spent two decades building environments that respond to, and quietly undo, the architecture around them.

Inside, vitrines and new plaster-and-wood paintings extend Djordjadze's long engagement with modernist design's leftover forms — the vitrine as a display device stripped of anything to protect, the wooden frame packed with worked, layered pigment until it sits somewhere between painting and relief. Her materials are deliberately modest (wood, plaster, paint, glass) and her forms often look unfinished or provisional, as though the room were still mid-renovation, which is part of the point: she's less interested in discrete objects than in the charged, unresolved space between them.

For an artist whose work draws on memory, domesticity and the half-remembered logic of interiors, a show titled after night and its wells feels apt — these are pieces built for dim, contemplative looking rather than declarative statement, and the gallery's intimate scale suits that quality well.

shows.title: Unnatural Habitat
shows.description:
Hiroshi Sugimoto's third solo show at Lisson returns to the body of work that made his name: black-and-white photographs of taxidermy dioramas at the American Museum of Natural History, a series he began in the mid-1970s and has quietly continued ever since. Lions, condors, jaguars, an early hominid, a cactus forest — Sugimoto photographs these constructed habitats so precisely that the seams between painted backdrop and stuffed animal disappear, and the image reads as a real, frozen moment of nature that never actually existed.

What makes this show more than a survey is the fifty-year time span it covers, from "Polar Bear" (1975), his very first work as an artist, through pictures he made at the museum again in 2025 — in one case going back to fix a lighting flaw in a diorama he'd shot decades earlier. New to the series are four color diorama images printed on washi paper as folding screens, or byōbu, made through traditional Kyoto craftsmanship — only the second time color has entered his photographic practice in any sustained way.

It's a rare chance to see the full arc of one of photography's most patient conceptual projects in one room, and the new screens suggest Sugimoto isn't done finding fresh formal problems inside a fifty-year-old idea.

shows.title: Leonilson
shows.description:
Leonilson died in 1993 at 36, and this show traces his short, restless career from teenage assemblage through the small embroidered textile works he made after his HIV diagnosis in 1991. It's organized with Projeto Leonilson and the São Paulo gallery Almeida & Dale, and it's a rare chance to see this material together in New York.

The early pieces show a Brazilian artist absorbing everything around him — the legacy of Hélio Oiticica and Lygia Clark, then later the graphic energy of Keith Haring and Basquiat during trips to the U.S. and Europe in the 1980s. But the show's emotional center is the late embroidery work, made after Leonilson could no longer tolerate toxic paint fumes: small pieces of voile, felt, and cotton sheeting stitched with single words or fragile diagrammatic images — maps, vessels, windows, his own name — that turn illness into a spare, private vocabulary.

Leonilson's reputation has grown steadily outside Brazil over the past decade, and this show — which moves from exuberant early collage to whisper-quiet late textiles — makes the case for him as one of the more original, least categorizable artists of his generation.

shows.title: American Progress (after John Gast)
shows.dates_note: Paula Cooper's page marks this vitrine installation "On View" with no closing date; the installation-view captions on the same page date the presentation to "June 22 - July 31, 2026," but the gallery has not listed a close.
shows.description:
Liz Glynn's American Progress (after John Gast) reworks the central figure from John Gast's 1872 painting American Progress — the allegorical woman who strides westward ahead of settlers, railroads, and telegraph wires as bison and Native people flee before her — into a hollow, disembodied shell of draped copper sheeting. Stripped of the body it once clothed, the dress becomes a monument to a myth rather than a person, copper doing double duty as a reference to both nineteenth-century industry and the Statue of Liberty.

The piece is part of Glynn's ongoing series The Shape of Progress and first appeared in her 2017–18 installation at Mass MoCA, The Archaeology of Another Possible Future, which imagined the wreckage of a dematerialized future economy. Installed now in Paula Cooper's vitrine during the 250th anniversary of the United States, the work reads as a pointed, quietly devastating retort to the idea of manifest destiny and unbroken national progress.

It's a small, single-work presentation, but a dense one — a good entry point into Glynn's longstanding interest in sculpture as a vehicle for historical critique, using industrial material to hollow out a foundational American image.

shows.title: Octopus
shows.description:
Ross Bleckner's fourth solo show with Petzel gathers new paintings built from an accumulating private archive of images — clippings from newspapers, books, and the internet, plus his own daily observations — that he treats not as sources to reproduce but as material to be mutated across canvases. One painting leads to the next by association rather than plan, so that motifs drift between recognizable and abstract from work to work.

In Medicine Cabinet, a web of biomorphic forms and branching red lines reads simultaneously as anatomical diagram, circulatory system, and architectural plan; in Where Is My Body, pale pink linear structures float across luminous blue-and-white fields somewhere between molecular model and crystal lattice. The title painting, The Dancers, dissolves the figure entirely into overlapping gestural layers until bodies register only as movement.

Bleckner has spent decades working this territory between figuration and abstraction, often circling around the body without depicting it directly, and this show is a good measure of how that ambiguity keeps generating new formal possibilities four decades into his career.

shows.title: Transit of Venus
shows.description:
Emily Mae Smith's second solo show at Petzel pushes her recurring cast of hybrid characters — the anthropomorphic broomstick, disembodied eyeballs, open-mouthed frames — further into unstable, part-human, part-plant, part-animal territory. Rather than functioning as fixed metaphors, these trickster figures resist easy classification, positioned by Smith as active agents rather than passive symbols within paintings that draw equally on Pop Art, Surrealism, and nineteenth-century genre painting.

In The Locust II, Smith's signature broomstick morphs into a scythe-wielding figure emerging from straw, inverting the passive reclining nude of academic painting into an armed, watchful presence. In Only Human, brightly colored grapes each sprout a single eyeball, a send-up of ocularcentrism and the way selfhood gets negotiated under constant observation. Smith builds her glassy, luminous surfaces through patient layers of glaze, a technical rigor that sits at odds with the impishness of her subject matter.

Following her 2024 survey alongside René Magritte at the Magritte Museum in Brussels, this show finds Smith working at full confidence, using inherited painterly languages to needle at very contemporary anxieties about power, gender, and the erosion of individual agency.

shows.title: Form, Shadow, Motion: Selections from the Burger Collection, Hong Kong
shows.description:
Curator Olivia Shao pulls roughly fifty works on paper from the Burger Collection's holding of over a thousand drawings, assembling a cross-generational, cross-continental essay that sets Hong Kong and New York up as twin poles of reference. The artist list runs from Meret Oppenheim and Blinky Palermo to Jack Whitten, Robert Gober, Alicja Kwade, and a strong cohort of Hong Kong-based artists including Kong Chun Hei and Koon Wai Bong — twenty-nine artists in all, spanning decades and continents.

Rather than a survey organized by geography or period, the show is built around shared philosophical undercurrents — Eastern thought and Western abstraction read against each other — and will occupy the entirety of the Drawing Center's galleries before traveling to Asia Society Hong Kong in an expanded form in 2027. It's a rare chance to see a serious private collection's holdings in dialogue rather than as a simple checklist.

shows.title: Medley
shows.description:
Medley is Parisian artist Pablo Tomek's first New York solo, introducing in person a practice that most local audiences will only have encountered on a screen. Tomek comes out of graffiti, and that background is legible in the physicality of his method: paintings built through repeated cycles of addition and removal, worked over with industrial sponges and blasted with high-pressure water until the surface reads as excavated as much as painted.

The sculptural side of the show extends that same logic — pieces that mimic the raw, half-finished look of sheetrock mudding, doubling as seating and underlining the sense that everything here is caught mid-process rather than resolved. Tomek has shown at Palais de Tokyo and with galleries in Paris, Brussels, and Cologne, and was included in last year's Bold & Gritty survey at Amsterdam's Stedelijk Museum; this is a chance to see the surface effects that define his work — the layering, the abrasion, the evidence of process — at full scale and up close.

shows.title: Voices in the Mirror
shows.description:
Marking the 20th anniversary of The Gordon Parks Foundation, this exhibition takes a different approach to a much-exhibited archive: rather than presenting Parks's photographs on the strength of their formal power alone, it surrounds them with first-person reflections from the people he photographed and their families. Images that have been reproduced for decades — a boy pointing to a white doll in the 1947 "doll test" photographs, a girl helped up to a segregated water fountain in 1956 Alabama, Eldridge and Kathleen Cleaver in exile in Algiers — are re-anchored to the memories of Kate Clark Harris, Cora Taylor, Kathleen Cleaver, and others who lived inside those frames.

The gallery has also gathered reflections from a wider circle touched by Parks's legacy: Lonnie Ali, Qubilah Shabazz, Anderson Cooper, Isabella Rossellini, Ava DuVernay, Bryan Stevenson, and Alice and Rebecca Walker among them. The effect is less a retrospective than an oral history built around photographs — a way of returning agency and specificity to subjects who are otherwise remembered mainly as evidence of an era.

Parks, who died in 2006, remains one of the towering figures of twentieth-century American photography and one of the few photojournalists whose work moved as easily through Life magazine assignments as through fiction, memoir, and film (he wrote and directed Shaft). This show's premise — that his photographs were always collaborative, dependent on relationships built with subjects rather than just an eye for composition — is a useful corrective to seeing him purely as a documentarian of Black life from the outside.

shows.title: Memory of the Surface
shows.description:
Vicky Colombet's first solo exhibition with the gallery presents paintings that behave more like geological or atmospheric processes than depictions of them. Working with raw pigment ground by hand and floated in oil and solvent, Colombet lays her canvases flat and lets gravity, chemistry, and the particular weight of each mineral do much of the compositional work — a method refined over five decades that she connects explicitly to her long practice of Buddhist meditation and a deliberate quieting of her own hand.

The results read simultaneously as abstraction and as landscape: ultramarine blue fracturing across raw linen like a river delta seen from above, silver surfaces built from a decade-long series responding to melting polar ice, luminous centers that nod to her ongoing dialogue with Monet (whose work the Musée Marmottan Monet paired directly with hers in a rare 2020 exhibition for a living artist). Raised in Paris between a French father and a Filipino mother, with a childhood spent traveling through Southeast Asia and India, Colombet folds an early exposure to Buddhist philosophy into a studio practice that treats the painting's surface as something to be entered rather than read.

It's slow, absorptive work that rewards standing close and then stepping back — up close the paint reads as pure incident, from across the room as topography.

shows.title: Untitled (Gökhun Baltacı solo exhibition)
shows.dates_note: Venue's own upcoming-exhibitions page lists only "opening september 9th, 2026, kaufmann repetto new york" with no stated closing date
shows.description:
Turkish painter Gökhun Baltacı works almost exclusively in oil pastel, building cohesive, novelistic bodies of work from a recurring cast of everyday objects — a table, a cassette tape, a comb, a chestnut — that migrate between compositions like characters moving between rooms. His pictures read less as single images than as pages of one long, elliptical narrative: a muted, earthy palette holds scenes together even as the relationships between them stay deliberately unresolved.

Baltacı, who grew up in Ankara and trained at Hacettepe University before relocating to Paris's Cité internationale des arts, first showed this body of work in Milan; this is his New York gallery debut. Expect the same close, patient attention to overlooked domestic detail — a fence glimpsed through a window, the fold in a tablecloth — that critics have singled out as the real engine of his pictures, along with occasional ruptures where a hidden violence (a bleeding bird, a flute as weapon) breaks the quiet surface.

Given his materials and his slow, cumulative way of building meaning, this is a show best absorbed by spending real time in the room rather than passing through quickly.

shows.title: Brujas
shows.description:
Tamara Gonzales has spent decades building paintings out of materials more associated with lived, domestic culture than with fine art — lace doilies used as spray paint stencils, embroidery patterns, graffiti gesture — layering them into dense, decorative compositions that resist any clean separation between "high" and "low" sources. Brujas (Spanish for witches) continues that project, and the title suggests a turn toward the folkloric and the ritual, consistent with a practice already steeped in Mesoamerican cosmology (a previous show was titled after the Aztec creator deity Ometeotl).

Born in Madera, California in 1959 and based in Brooklyn, Gonzales has had solo shows at Klaus von Nichtssagend going back to 2014, and her work is held in the collections of the High Museum and the Bronx Museum. Her paintings typically reward close looking — the lace-stencil patterns read as ornament from a distance but reveal odd, almost occult repetitions up close, an effect that has drawn comparisons to devotional and outsider traditions as much as to painterly abstraction.

This is a gallery that has shown her consistently for over a decade, and Brujas looks to be a continuation and deepening of a well-established visual vocabulary rather than a sharp departure.

shows.title: The Prime of Your Life
shows.description:
The Prime of Your Life is a group exhibition built entirely around a single, blunt curatorial premise: every artist in it is a woman over 75 whose work continues to reshape contemporary art. The roster is a who's-who of postwar art history still very much in production — Marina Abramović, Lynda Benglis, Judy Chicago, Jenny Holzer, Mary Heilmann, Martha Rosler, Rose Wylie, and Sonia Gomes among them — spanning performance documentation, sculpture, textile, and painting.

Rather than framing longevity as a retrospective footnote, the show argues for it as an active condition — these are artists still setting terms for what their mediums can do, decades into practices that in several cases predate most contemporary galleries' existence. Given the range of the group, expect a wide swing in material and tone, from Holzer's text-based provocations to Benglis's poured and knotted forms to Wylie's loose, oversized figuration.

It's an ambitious, crowded premise for a gallery show, and worth seeing precisely for how directly it makes its point: that sustained, undiminished ambition is its own subject.

shows.title: SI OFFSITE | Rafał Skoczek: Kino Drift
shows.description:
With its St Marks Place home closed for a multi-year rebuild, Swiss Institute is spending 2026 as an itinerant organization, and this offsite project turns that condition into the show itself. Zurich-based artist Rafał Skoczek takes over a studio floor at WSA on Water Street and rebuilds it as a semi-permanent set: paintings, furniture, and display structures that double as seating, shelving, and screens, all designed to be rearranged as the exhibition is used rather than simply viewed.

Rather than a fixed hang, Kino Drift unfolds as a running program - film screenings organized with the Zurich collective Filmclub Populaire, a print and reading room stocked with small-press books and ephemera Skoczek has collected over years, meetings of a Badiou-focused reading group, and a chess-and-noise event called Chess Noise staged with musician Jeff Witscher. The music side runs under Czarnagora, the label and concert series Skoczek co-founded with Sem Lala.

It's a fitting register for an artist whose work has always treated exhibition-making, publishing, and music as inseparable activities rather than separate disciplines. Coming from someone who has co-run artist spaces like UP STATE and Chickentown, the piece reads less as a static installation than as a working social infrastructure - a temporary clubhouse assembled out of painting, carpentry, and programming that changes shape the longer it stays open.

shows.title: Mieko Meguro: Works, New York, 2009-2026 / Eric Spencer: Words on my Mind / Juliette Collet: Bobbie Cadet in the Court of the Ladybugs
shows.artist: Mieko Meguro, Eric Spencer, Juliette Collet
shows.description:
White Columns opens its 2026/27 season with three simultaneous, unrelated solo presentations, a format the space has used for decades to give emerging and overlooked artists equal billing on the same visit. Mieko Meguro's contribution surveys nearly two decades of her New York work, from 2009 to the present, promising a rare long view of a practice that has developed largely outside the gallery-show cycle. Eric Spencer's Words on My Mind draws on his vintage color photography - the one available image, an untitled picture of a boy labeled "FEAR" against a suburban backdrop, has the deadpan, slightly uncanny documentary quality that suggests a body of vernacular-inflected image-making. Juliette Collet's Bobbie Cadet in the Court of the Ladybugs rounds out the trio with a title that hints at the kind of invented, storybook logic White Columns has long made room for.

Shown together rather than sequentially, the three artists have little in common stylistically, which is very much the point of White Columns' program: a photographer's decades-spanning archive, a single body of color photographs, and an artist working in a more fabulist register, all sharing the same rooms. It's a useful season opener for taking the temperature of what the city's oldest alternative space is paying attention to right now.
